q: When something worth keeping is said, what should trigger the write?
a: Context scarcity.

q: Who has authority to write to memory: the model, a deterministic component, or the user?
a: The model, alone.

q: What happens to raw input after it's been used?
a: Kept forever.

q: What is the unit of a memory: an utterance, or a claim assembled from several?
a: An utterance or a short agent-authored line.

q: What shape should durable memory have: text the model writes for itself, or records something else can read?
a: A fixed-size read/write block of unstructured text, editable only through function calls (§2.1). No fields, no ids, no timestamps, no source, no confidence.

q: On what basis should memory be split into stores?
a: By origin.

q: When a fact enters memory, what should record how much the system is entitled to believe it?
a: Nothing. Everything in working context is a flat assertion in the same voice.

q: Whose facts is the system storing?
a: Anyone's.

q: What should cause information to leave the working set?
a: Token thresholds. Warn at ~70%, flush at 100%, evict ~50% of the window (§2.2). Recency determines what goes.

q: When information has to be compressed, what should the compressed form be?
a: A recursive summary — the previous summary plus the newly evicted messages, regenerated at each flush and parked at the head of the queue (§2.1–2.2).

q: When new information contradicts something stored, what happens to the old version?
a: It's overwritten.

q: What has to be true for a contradiction to be noticed at all?
a: The old fact must already be in the context window, and the model must happen to spot the conflict mid-conversation.

q: What should determine which memories come back for a given request?
a: Embedding cosine similarity, pgvector + HNSW over ada-002 vectors, paginated (§3.2.1).

q: Who decides when enough has been retrieved?
a: The model, by choosing whether to request another page (§2.3–2.4, function chaining via request_heartbeat).

q: Should being retrieved and being usable be the same thing?
a: Yes, necessarily.

q: How much of the memory system should the user be able to see?
a: None of it.

q: Should the system volunteer what it remembers, or wait to be asked?
a: Volunteer, enthusiastically.

q: When memory doesn't contain the answer, what should the system do?
a: Guess. The MemGPT persona is instructed to "reply with a best guess using the information in core memory" and conversation search (Appendix 6.1.1).

q: When a stored memory is wrong, how does it get fixed?
a: Only if the model notices and rewrites it (D11).

q: What should happen to a memory that hasn't been relevant in a long time?
a: Nothing. Working-context entries persist until explicitly overwritten; recall storage is kept indefinitely (§2.2).
